claims.wording: In October 1603 there was fighting at Manila between Chinese residents and the Spaniards. It ended in the killing of very many of the Chinese of Manila by Spanish soldiers and by the Japanese soldiers and the men of Pampanga and the Tagalog provinces who fought beside them. Historians give different totals. Borao writes that some 20,000 were killed. Wills writes of more than twenty thousand, and says estimates range from fifteen thousand to twenty-five thousand. Borao reports that the Ming Shi gives twenty-five thousand. Spanish and Chinese records tell the same events in the same order.
claims.notes:
Quote: "put down by the Spanish who, together with Philippine and Japanese troops, massacred some 20,000 Chinese" (Borao 1998, p. 22); "chronicles in both languages include the same facts and are alike in the ordering of events" (Borao 1998, p. 22); "A new detachment of Spaniards, Japanese and 1500 natives of Pampanga and the Tagalog provinces is formed in Manila." (Borao 1998, p. 30); "Twenty five thousand Chinese perished in the massacre." (Borao 1998, p. 31); "a massacre in which more than twenty thousand Chinese were killed" (Wills 2010, p. 56); "Estimates of the total number of Chinese slaughtered range from fifteen thousand to twenty-five thousand." (Wills 2010, p. 58); "as Filipino auxiliaries arrived from outlying areas the Chinese broke and fled" (Wills 2010, p. 58)

claims.wording: The Spanish writers say the Chinese of Manila rose. Archbishop Benavides wrote that a rumour had spread among them that the Spaniards meant to kill them all. Governor Acuña told the king it had been stirred up from China. A historian notes that the testimony behind that charge was taken under torture.
claims.notes:
Quote: "The Spanish sources (Morga, Argensola, Acuña, etc.) emphatically state that the Chinese staged an uprising." (Borao 1998, p. 29); "that the Spanish were going to kill every one of them" (Borao 1998, quoting Benavides, p. 29); "it goes without saying that the uprising was instigated from China" (Borao 1998, quoting Acuña, p. 29); "their validity is doubtful since they were obtained through torture" (Borao 1998, p. 31); "persuading them that the precautions and measures which I was taking were in order to kill them" (Acuña, p. 154); "his eventual moves, preventive and defensive in nature" (Borao 1998, p. 28)

claims.wording: In May 1603 three Ming officials came to Manila to look for a mountain said to yield gold. Spanish and Chinese records both name this visit as what set off the Spaniards' fear of an invasion.
claims.notes:
Quote: "Three mandarins landed in Manila, displaying their insignias as judges." (Borao 1998, p. 26); "this trip had been the cause of the Spanish suspicions and the subsequent massacre four months later" (Borao 1998, p. 28)

confidence.rationale: high that Borao says it. He builds the timeline from Argensola and two judges hostile to the governor, and says the events 'might have taken place as follows' (p. 26). John Wills gives a different list: 'An assistant xian magistrate, Wang Shihe, and a company commander, Yu Yicheng', arriving in March 1603, with a second meeting in May (Wills 2010, p. 57). Borao's third official is his own inference from a name in the letter (p. 27).

claims.wording: The Ming emperor, in the official history, said that the governor of Luzon had killed people without leave. The governor of Fujian, Xu Xueju, wrote to Manila demanding that the widows and children of the dead be sent home. China sent no fleet.
claims.notes:
Quote: "the governor of Luzon murdered people without license" (Borao 1998, translating the *Ming Shi*, p. 32); "demanding that the widows and children of the victims be sent back to China" (Borao 1998, p. 32); "For the moment, China did not launch a punitive attack" (Borao 1998, p. 32)
